cards.title: Partition norm and Riemann sums
cards.body: For a partition \(\mathcal{P} = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n)\) of \([a,b]\), the norm \(\|\mathcal{P}\|\) is the largest subinterval length \(\max(x_i - x_{i-1})\).

cards.title: Step functions and finite changes
cards.body: Every step function on \([a,b]\) is Riemann integrable. By Theorem 7.1.3, changing a function at finitely many points never alters its integrability or integral.

cards.title: Lebesgue's Integrability Criterion
cards.body: A bounded function \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{R}[a,b]\) if and only if its set of discontinuities is a null set (measure zero).

cards.title: Differentiating variable-limit integrals
cards.body: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(v : [c,d] \to [a,b]\) is differentiable, the Second Fundamental Theorem and Chain Rule give the derivative of \(G(x) = \int_a^{v(x)} f\).

phases.name: Split
phases.why: break the integral at basepoint 0

phases.name: Primitive
phases.why: express both integrals using F

phases.name: Differentiate
phases.why: differentiate with respect to x

phases.name: Apply FTC
phases.why: replace F' with f

steps.note: Split \(\int_{x-c}^{x+c} f(t)\,dt\) at \(0\) using Theorem 7.2.13.
Reverse limits on the first integral: \(\int_{x-c}^0 f = -\int_0^{x-c} f\).

ask.q: How do we write \(\int_{x-c}^0 f(t)\,dt\) with lower limit \(0\)?
ask.why: By Definition 7.2.12, swapping integration limits changes the sign.

steps.note: Write each integral in terms of the indefinite integral \(F\).
Apply the Chain Rule; \(\frac{d}{dx}(x \pm c) = 1\).
By Theorem 7.3.6, \(F'(u) = f(u)\) everywhere since \(f\) is continuous.

ask.q: Why does \(F'(u) = f(u)\) hold for every \(u \in \mathbb{R}\)?
options: By the Fundamental Theorem (Second Form), since \(f\) is continuous
Because every integrable function is differentiable
By the Squeeze Theorem for step functions
ask.why: Theorem 7.3.6 guarantees that the indefinite integral of a continuous function \(f\) has derivative \(f\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Modified step function (Ex. 7.1.6b)
cards.body: For \(h(x) = 2\) on \([0,1)\), \(h(1) = 3\), and \(h(x) = 1\) on \((1,2]\), the single value \(h(1) = 3\) does not change the integral.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: On \(I = [0, 4]\), what is the norm \(\|\mathcal{P}_3\|\) of the partition \(\mathcal{P}_3 = (0, 1, 1.5, 2, 3.4, 4)\)?
cards.why: The subinterval lengths are \(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1.4, 0.6\), and their maximum is \(1.4\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Lebesgue's Integrability Criterion, a bounded function on \([a,b]\) is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuities is a ______ set.
cards.why: Theorem 7.3.12 states that a bounded function is in \(\mathcal{R}[a,b]\) iff it is continuous almost everywhere, meaning its discontinuities form a null set.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, 4]\) and partition \(\mathcal{P}_1 = (0, 1, 2, 4)\) with tags at the left endpoints, calculate the Riemann sum \(S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_1)\).

cards.title: Pointwise convergence
cards.body: A sequence of functions \((f_n)\) on \(A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) converges pointwise on \(A_0 \subseteq A\) to \(f\) if for each fixed \(x \in A_0\), the numerical sequence \((f_n(x))\) converges to \(f(x)\).

cards.title: The \(\varepsilon\)-\(K(\varepsilon, x)\) criterion
cards.body: By Lemma 8.1.3, \(f_n \to f\) on \(A_0\) iff for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) and each \(x \in A_0\), there is a natural number \(K(\varepsilon, x)\) such that \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon\) for all \(n \ge K(\varepsilon, x)\).

cards.title: The power sequence \(g_n(x) = x^n\)
cards.body: For \(g_n(x) = x^n\), we have \(x^n \to 0\) when \(-1 < x < 1\) and \(1^n \to 1\) at \(x = 1\). At \(x = -1\) or \(|x| > 1\), the sequence diverges, so the domain of convergence is \((-1, 1]\).

phases.name: Error
phases.why: write distance from f_N(x) to limit 0

phases.name: Threshold
phases.why: set error equal to epsilon at cutoff N

phases.name: Clear fraction
phases.why: multiply by x + N

phases.name: Isolate N
phases.why: solve for N in terms of x and epsilon

steps.note: For \(x > 0\), the pointwise limit of \(\frac{x}{x+N}\) is \(0\).
Simplify the error expression.
Find the cutoff index \(N\) where the error equals \(\varepsilon\).
Multiply both sides by \(x + N > 0\).

ask.q: How do we bring \(N\) out of the denominator?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(x + N\) clears the denominator.

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(\varepsilon > 0\).
Subtract \(x\) from both sides to isolate \(N\).

ask.q: What happens to the required cutoff \(N\) as \(x \to \infty\) for a fixed \(\varepsilon \in (0, 1)\)?
ask.why: Since \(N = x(1/\varepsilon - 1)\), larger values of \(x\) require larger \(N\).

steps.note: The cutoff \(K(\varepsilon, x)\) grows linearly with \(x\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Piecewise limit (Ex. 8.1.4)
cards.body: For \(x > 1\), dividing numerator and denominator by \(x^n\) gives \(\frac{1}{x^{-n} + 1} \to 1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the largest subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) on which \(g_n(x) = x^n\) converges pointwise?
cards.why: The sequence \((x^n)\) converges to \(0\) on \((-1, 1)\) and to \(1\) at \(x = 1\), but oscillates at \(x = -1\) and is unbounded for \(|x| > 1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), what is the pointwise limit of \(f_n(x) = \operatorname{Arctan}(nx)\) as \(n \to \infty\)?
cards.why: As \(n \to \infty\), \(nx \to +\infty\) for \(x > 0\) (giving \(\pi/2\)), \(0\) for \(x = 0\) (giving \(0\)), and \(-\infty\) for \(x < 0\) (giving \(-\pi/2\)).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In Lemma 8.1.3 for pointwise convergence, the natural number \(K(\varepsilon, x)\) depends in general on both \(\varepsilon\) and ______.
cards.why: In pointwise convergence, the rate of convergence varies from point to point, so \(K\) depends on both \(\varepsilon\) and \(x\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For \(f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{1 + x^n}\), what is the value of the pointwise limit \(f(1) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(1)\)?
cards.why: At \(x = 1\), \(f_n(1) = \frac{1^n}{1 + 1^n} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\) for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

cards.title: Uniform convergence
cards.body: A sequence \((f_n)\) converges uniformly on \(A_0\) to \(f\) (written \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\)) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a \(K(\varepsilon)\) independent of \(x \in A_0\) such that \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon\) for all \(n \ge K(\varepsilon)\).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Function f_n inside an epsilon band around limit f"><path d="M 25 90 Q 130 40 235 80 L 235 130 Q 130 90 25 140 Z" class="s"/><path d="M 25 115 Q 130 65 235 105" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 25 122 Q 130 52 235 98" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="25" y1="160" x2="235" y2="160" class="gk" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="242" y="108" font-size="13" class="t">f</text><text x="130" y="32" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" class="t">epsilon tube</text></svg>

cards.title: Uniform norm on a set
cards.body: For a bounded function \(\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}\), the uniform norm is \(\|\varphi\|_A := \sup\{|\varphi(x)| : x \in A\}\). By Lemma 8.1.8, \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\) on \(A\) iff \(\|f_n - f\|_A \to 0\).

cards.title: Non-uniformity and Cauchy Criterion
cards.body: By Lemma 8.1.5, \(f_n \not\rightrightarrows f\) if there exist \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\), a subsequence \((f_{n_k})\), and \(x_k \in A_0\) with \(|f_{n_k}(x_k) - f(x_k)| \ge \varepsilon_0\). By Theorem 8.1.10, bounded \((f_n)\) converge uniformly iff \(\|f_m - f_n\|_A \to 0\).

phases.name: Expand
phases.why: write G_n as a polynomial in x

phases.name: Differentiate
phases.why: find derivative G_n'(x)

phases.name: Critical point
phases.why: set derivative equal to 0

phases.name: Solve
phases.why: isolate the maximizer x

steps.note: Expand \(x^n(1 - x)\) on \([0, 1]\) to differentiate term by term.
Differentiate with respect to \(x\) to find the maximum on \([0,1]\).

ask.q: How do we find the interior point where \(|G_n(x) - 0|\) attains its supremum on \([0, 1]\)?
options: Differentiate \(G_n(x)\) with respect to \(x\) and solve \(G_n'(x) = 0\)
ask.why: Since \(G_n(0) = G_n(1) = 0\) and \(G_n(x) > 0\) on \((0,1)\), its maximum occurs at an interior critical point.

steps.note: Factor out \(x^{n-1}\).
Set \(G_n'(x) = 0\) on the open interval \((0, 1)\).
Since \(x \in (0, 1)\), \(x^{n-1} \neq 0\) cancels.
Move \((n+1)x\) to the left side.

options: It converges to \(1/e\), so convergence is not uniform
It stays equal to \(1\) for all \(n\)
ask.why: Since \((1+1/n)^{-n} \to 1/e\) and \(1/(n+1) \to 0\), their product tends to \(0\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Uniform norm on a bounded interval (Ex. 8.1.9c)
cards.body: For \(h_n(x) = \frac{x^2 + nx}{n}\) and \(h(x) = x\), convergence is not uniform on \(\mathbb{R}\), but is uniform on \([0, 8]\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: On \(A = [0, 1]\), what is the uniform norm \(\|g_n - g\|_A\) for \(g_n(x) = x^n\) and its pointwise limit \(g\)?
cards.why: On \([0, 1)\), \(|g_n(x) - g(x)| = x^n\), whose supremum is \(1\). Since \(1 \not\to 0\), \(g_n\) does not converge uniformly on \([0, 1]\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Let \(f_n(x) = x + \frac{1}{n}\) and \(f(x) = x\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) (Exercise 8.1.22). Which statement is true?
options: \((f_n)\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb{R}\), but \((f_n^2)\) does not
\((f_n^2)\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb{R}\), but \((f_n)\) does not
cards.why: We have \(\|f_n - f\|_{\mathbb{R}} = 1/n \to 0\), whereas \(|f_n^2(x) - f^2(x)| = |\frac{2x}{n} + \frac{1}{n^2}|\) is unbounded on \(\mathbb{R}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Lemma 8.1.8, a sequence of bounded functions \((f_n)\) on \(A\) converges uniformly to \(f\) if and only if the ______ norm \(\|f_n - f\|_A\) converges to \(0\).
cards.why: The supremum \(\|f_n - f\|_A = \sup\{|f_n(x) - f(x)| : x \in A\}\) is called the uniform norm on \(A\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For \(h_n(x) = \frac{x^2 + nx}{n}\) and \(h(x) = x\) on \(A = [0, 8]\), what is the uniform norm \(\|h_n - h\|_A\) when \(n = 16\)?
cards.why: Since \(|h_n(x) - h(x)| = x^2/n\) attains its supremum on \([0, 8]\) at \(x = 8\), \(\|h_{16} - h\|_A = 64/16 = 4\).

cards.title: When limit interchange fails
cards.body: If \(f_n \to f\) only pointwise, the limit function \(f\) need not preserve continuity, differentiability, or the value of the Riemann integral \(\lim \int_a^b f_n\).

cards.title: Loss of continuity and derivative
cards.body: In Example 8.2.1(a)-(b), each \(g_n(x) = x^n\) is continuous and differentiable on \([0,1]\), yet the pointwise limit \(g(x)\) jumps at \(x = 1\) and has no derivative there.

cards.title: Triangular spike functions (Ex. 8.2.1c)
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Tall narrow triangle spike function of area 1"><line x1="30" y1="145" x2="235" y2="145" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="30" y1="20" x2="30" y2="145" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="30,145 65,25 100,145" class="s ok" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="30,145 65,25 100,145 225,145" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="65" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">(1/n, n)</text><text x="100" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">2/n</text><text x="225" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">1</text></svg>

phases.name: Setup
phases.why: write the definite integral I_n

phases.name: Antiderivative
phases.why: express integrand as H_n'(x)

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.why: apply the Fundamental Theorem on [0,1]

phases.name: Simplify
phases.why: compute endpoint values

steps.note: Consider the smooth sequence \(h_n(x) = 2nxe^{-nx^2}\) on \([0, 1]\).
Notice that \(H_n(x) = -e^{-nx^2}\) has derivative \(H_n'(x) = 2nxe^{-nx^2}\).

ask.q: Which function \(H_n(x)\) is an antiderivative of \(h_n(x) = 2nxe^{-nx^2}\)?

steps.note: Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First Form).
Substitute \(x = 1\) and \(x = 0\) into \(-e^{-nx^2}\).
As \(n \to \infty\), \(I_n \to 1\), whereas \(\int_0^1 (\lim h_n) = 0\).

ask.q: Since \(h_n(x) \to 0\) pointwise on \([0, 1]\), what does \(I_n = 1 - e^{-n} \to 1\) show?
options: \(\int_0^1 (\lim h_n) = 0 \neq 1 = \lim \int_0^1 h_n\), so limit and integral do not commute here
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus fails for \(h_n\)
ask.why: Pointwise convergence alone does not allow interchanging the limit and the Riemann integral.

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Area of the spike function (Ex. 8.2.1c)
cards.body: Each triangle has base \(2/n\) and height \(n\), keeping area \(1\) even though \(f_n(x) \to 0\) for every \(x \in [0, 1]\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 8.2.1(c), why does the spike function \(f_n(x)\) converge pointwise to \(0\) for every \(x \in [0, 1]\)?
options: \(f_n(0) = 0\) for all \(n\), and for any \(x > 0\), \(f_n(x) = 0\) whenever \(n > 2/x\)
The maximum height \(n\) tends to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\)
The sequence \((f_n)\) is uniformly bounded on \([0, 1]\)

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For \(h_n(x) = 2nxe^{-nx^2}\) on \([0, 1]\), what are \(\int_0^1 (\lim h_n(x))\,dx\) and \(\lim \int_0^1 h_n(x)\,dx\) respectively?
cards.why: Since \(h_n(x) \to 0\) for each \(x \in [0, 1]\), \(\int_0^1 (\lim h_n) = 0\), while \(\int_0^1 h_n = 1 - e^{-n} \to 1\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Example 8.2.1(c) shows a sequence of continuous functions converging nonuniformly to \(f(x) = 0\), proving that uniform convergence is sufficient but not ______ for the limit function to be continuous.
cards.why: As noted in the Remark to Theorem 8.2.2 and Exercise 8.2.2, uniform convergence is sufficient but not necessary for a continuous limit.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In Example 8.2.1(c), what is the maximum value \(\|f_5\|_{[0,1]}\) attained by \(f_5(x)\) at \(x = 1/5\)?
cards.why: At \(x = 1/n\), \(f_n(1/n) = n^2(1/n) = n\), so for \(n = 5\) the peak height is \(5\).

cards.title: Uniform limit of continuous functions
cards.body: Theorem 8.2.2 states that if \((f_n)\) is a sequence of continuous functions on a set \(A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\) uniformly on \(A\), then \(f\) is continuous on \(A\).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Three-part epsilon over 3 triangle inequality bound"><path d="M 30 135 Q 130 95 230 45" class="lk" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 30 120 Q 130 80 230 60" class="hk" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="95" cy="108" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="95" cy="94" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="165" cy="78" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="165" cy="72" r="4" class="f"/><line x1="95" y1="94" x2="95" y2="155" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="165" y1="72" x2="165" y2="155" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="95" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" class="t">c</text><text x="165" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" class="t">x</text><text x="236" y="48" font-size="13" class="t">f</text><text x="236" y="66" font-size="13" class="t">f_H</text></svg>

cards.title: The \(\varepsilon/3\) proof strategy
cards.body: We fix \(H\) so \(\|f_H - f\|_A < \varepsilon/3\), then use continuity of \(f_H\) at \(c\) to find \(\delta > 0\) with \(|f_H(x) - f_H(c)| < \varepsilon/3\). The Triangle Inequality gives \(|f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\).

cards.title: Contrapositive and sequential tests
cards.body: If every \(f_n\) is continuous on \(A\) but the pointwise limit \(f\) is discontinuous on \(A\), then \(f_n \not\rightrightarrows f\) on \(A\). Also, if \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\) on \(I\) and \(x_n \to x_0 \in I\), then \(\lim f_n(x_n) = f(x_0)\).

cards.title: Boundedness preservation (Ex. 8.2.7)
cards.body: If \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\) on \(A\) and each \(f_n\) is bounded on \(A\), then \(f\) is bounded on \(A\). Consequently, if the pointwise limit \(f\) is unbounded on \(A\), convergence cannot be uniform.

phases.name: Start
phases.why: write f_n(x) for x > 0

phases.name: Rescale
phases.why: divide numerator and denominator by n

phases.name: Pass to limit
phases.why: let 1/n tend to 0 as n tends to infinity

phases.name: Simplify
phases.why: cancel x to reveal the unbounded limit 1/x

steps.note: Each \(f_n\) is bounded on \(A = [0, \infty)\) with maximum \(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}\).

move.label: Divide top and bottom by n

steps.note: Divide numerator and denominator by \(n\) for \(x > 0\).

ask.q: For fixed \(x > 0\), how do we evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{nx}{1 + nx^2}\)?
options: Take the derivative with respect to \(x\)
ask.why: Dividing top and bottom by \(n\) isolates \(1/n\), which tends to \(0\).

steps.note: As \(n \to \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \to 0\) while \(x > 0\) is fixed.
Since \(f(x) = 1/x\) for \(x > 0\) is unbounded on \([0, \infty)\), \(f_n \not\rightrightarrows f\).

ask.q: Since each \(f_n\) is bounded on \([0, \infty)\) and \(f(x) = 1/x\) for \(x > 0\), why does \((f_n)\) fail to converge uniformly on \([0, \infty)\)?
options: By Exercise 8.2.7, a uniform limit of bounded functions must be bounded, but \(f\) is unbounded near \(0\)
ask.why: Both Theorem 8.2.2 (discontinuity at \(0\)) and Exercise 8.2.7 (unbounded limit) rule out uniform convergence on \([0, \infty)\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Discontinuity rules out uniform convergence (Ex. 8.2.1)
cards.tex: f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{x^n}{1 + x^n} \text{ jumps at } x = 1 \implies f_n \not\rightrightarrows f \text{ on } [0, 2]
cards.body: Each \(f_n\) is continuous on \([0, 2]\), but \(f(x)\) jumps from \(0\) to \(1/2\) to \(1\) at \(x = 1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In the proof of Theorem 8.2.2, why can we choose a single index \(H\) such that \(|f(x) - f_H(x)| < \varepsilon/3\) and \(|f_H(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon/3\) for all \(x \in A\)?
options: Because \(A\) must be a closed bounded interval
cards.why: Uniform convergence gives a single index \(H = H(\varepsilon/3)\) that works simultaneously for every point in \(A\), including \(x\) and \(c\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Let \(f_n(x) = \frac{1}{(1+x)^n}\) for \(x \in [0, 1]\) (Exercise 8.2.6). What is its pointwise limit \(f\), and does \((f_n)\) converge uniformly on \([0, 1]\)?
options: \(f(0) = 1\) and \(f(x) = 0\) for \(x \in (0, 1]\); not uniform because \(f\) is discontinuous at \(0\)
\(f(0) = 1\) and \(f(x) = 0\) for \(x \in (0, 1]\); uniform because \([0, 1]\) is closed
cards.why: At \(x = 0\), \(f_n(0) = 1 \to 1\), while for \(x > 0\), \(1 + x > 1\) so \((1+x)^{-n} \to 0\). Since \(f\) is discontinuous at \(0\), Theorem 8.2.2 implies convergence is not uniform.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: If a sequence \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \(A\) and each \(f_n\) is bounded on \(A\), then the limit function \(f\) is ______ on \(A\).
cards.why: By Exercise 8.2.7, choosing \(H\) with \(\|f_H - f\|_A \le 1\) gives \(|f(x)| \le |f_H(x)| + 1 \le M_H + 1\) for all \(x \in A\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Suppose continuous functions \(f_n\) on \([0, 2]\) converge uniformly to \(f(x) = 3x^2 + 1\). If \(x_n = 1 + \frac{1}{n}\), what is \(\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x_n)\)?
cards.why: By Exercise 8.2.4, since \(f_n \rightrightarrows f\) and \(x_n \to 1\), \(\lim f_n(x_n) = f(1) = 3(1)^2 + 1 = 4\).

cards.title: Equivalence relation and left cosets
cards.body: For a subgroup \(H \le G\), the relation \(a \sim_L b\) iff \(a^{-1}b \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\). The equivalence class containing \(a\) is the left coset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

cards.title: Additive cosets in \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_n\)
cards.body: When the group operation is addition, the left coset of \(H\) containing \(m\) is written \(m + H = \{m + h \mid h \in H\}\). The cosets partition the group into disjoint sets.

cards.title: Right cosets and nonabelian groups
cards.body: The relation \(a \sim_R b\) iff \(ab^{-1} \in H\) yields right cosets \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\). In abelian groups \(aH = Ha\), but in nonabelian groups such as \(D_4\), left and right cosets can differ.

cards.title: Properties of coset partitions
cards.body: The subgroup \(H = eH\) is always a coset of itself. Two left cosets \(aH\) and \(bH\) are either identical (when \(b \in aH\)) or completely disjoint, and \(gH = Hg\) for all \(g\) iff \(g^{-1}hg \in H\).

cards.title: Transitivity of \(\sim_L\) and coset form (Thm 10.1)
cards.legend: \(H \le G\) subgroup, \(a, b, c \in G\) with \(a \sim_L b\) and \(b \sim_L c\), \(h_1, h_2 \in H\).

phases.name: First relation
phases.why: express a ~_L b using an element h_1 in H

phases.name: Coset form
phases.why: solve for b to show b = a h_1 in aH

phases.name: Second relation
phases.why: combine with b ~_L c where b^-1 c = h_2

phases.name: Transitivity
phases.why: isolate a^-1 c as a product in H

steps.note: Since \(a \sim_L b\), \(a^{-1}b\) equals some element \(h_1 \in H\).
Multiply on the left by \(a\); this shows \(b \in aH\).

ask.q: If \(a^{-1}b = h_1 \in H\), how do we isolate \(b\) to see the form of elements in the equivalence class of \(a\)?
options: Multiply both sides on the left by \(a\)
Multiply both sides on the right by \(a\)
ask.why: Left-multiplying by \(a\) uses \(aa^{-1} = e\) to give \(b = ah_1 \in aH\).

steps.note: Multiply on the right by \(h_2 = b^{-1}c \in H\).
Since \(b^{-1}c = h_2\), we have \(bh_2 = c\).
Since \(H\) is a subgroup, \(h_1h_2 \in H\), proving \(a \sim_L c\).

ask.q: Why does \(a^{-1}c = h_1h_2\) guarantee that \(a^{-1}c \in H\)?
options: Because \(H\) is a subgroup and is closed under the group operation
Because \(G\) is assumed to be abelian
Because \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are inverses of each other
ask.why: Closure of the subgroup \(H\) ensures that the product \(h_1h_2\) of two elements in \(H\) lies in \(H\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Cosets of \(\langle 3 \rangle\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\) (Ex. 10.3)
cards.body: These three cosets are disjoint and exhaust all \(18\) elements of \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). By Theorem 10.1, when do two elements \(a, b \in G\) belong to the same left coset of \(H\)?
cards.why: The equivalence relation defining left cosets is \(a \sim_L b \iff a^{-1}b \in H\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In the dihedral group \(D_4\) with subgroup \(H = \{\iota, \mu\}\), what are the left coset \(\rho H\) and right coset \(H\rho\) (Examples 10.5 & 10.12)?
cards.why: In \(D_4\), \(\rho\mu = \mu\rho^3\), so \(\rho\{\iota, \mu\} = \{\rho, \mu\rho^3\}\) while \(\{\iota, \mu\}\rho = \{\rho, \mu\rho\}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Because the relation \(\sim_L\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, it is an ______ relation and partitions \(G\) into disjoint cosets.
cards.why: Theorem 10.1 proves that \(\sim_L\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\), whose equivalence classes are the left cosets of \(H\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many distinct cosets does the subgroup \(\langle 6 \rangle\) have in \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\) (Exercise 10.4)?
cards.why: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\), \(\langle 6 \rangle = \{0, 6, 12\}\) has \(3\) elements, so it partitions \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\) into \(18 / 3 = 6\) cosets.

cards.title: Equal cardinality and Lagrange's Theorem
cards.body: The map \(f : H \to aH\) given by \(f(h) = ah\) is a bijection, so every coset of \(H\) has cardinality \(|H|\). If \(G\) is finite, \(|G| = r|H|\), so \(|H|\) divides \(|G|\).

cards.title: Prime order groups and element orders
cards.body: By Corollary 10.8, every group of prime order \(p\) is cyclic and isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_p\). By Theorem 10.9, the order of any element \(a\) of a finite group \(G\) divides \(|G|\).

cards.title: Index of a subgroup
cards.body: The index \((G : H)\) is the number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\). For finite \(G\), \((G : H) = |G|/|H|\). If \(K \le H \le G\) have finite indices, Theorem 10.11 gives \((G : K) = (G : H)(H : K)\).

cards.title: Converse of Lagrange's Theorem
cards.body: The converse of Lagrange's Theorem is false in general: a finite group need not have a subgroup of every order dividing \(|G|\). However, every finite abelian group has a subgroup of every divisor order.

cards.title: Proof that \(a^n = e\) in a group of order \(n\) (Ex. 10.42)
cards.legend: \(G\) finite group of order \(n\), \(a \in G\) element of order \(m = |\langle a \rangle|\), \(e\) identity.

phases.name: Lagrange
phases.why: relate group order n to element order m

phases.name: Substitute
phases.why: replace n with rm in the exponent of a

phases.name: Power law
phases.why: rewrite a^(rm) as a power of a^m

phases.name: Identity
phases.why: use a^m = e to simplify to e

steps.note: By Theorem 10.9, the order \(m = |\langle a \rangle|\) divides \(n = |G|\).
Replace the exponent \(n\) with \(rm\).

ask.q: Why does the order \(m\) of an element \(a \in G\) divide the order \(n\) of the finite group \(G\)?
options: Because \(m\) is the order of the cyclic subgroup \(\langle a \rangle \le G\), and \(|\langle a \rangle|\) divides \(|G|\) by Lagrange's Theorem
Because every finite group is cyclic
Because \(a\) commutes with every element of \(G\)
ask.why: By Theorem 10.9, the order of \(a\) equals the order of the cyclic subgroup \(\langle a \rangle\), which divides \(|G|\) by Theorem 10.7.

steps.note: Use the exponent rule \(a^{rm} = (a^m)^r\).
Since \(a\) has order \(m\), \(a^m = e\).

ask.q: What is the value of \(a^m\) when \(m\) is the order of \(a\)?
ask.why: By definition of element order, \(a^m = e\).

steps.note: Any power of the identity \(e\) is \(e\).

cards.label: Example
cards.title: Calculating subgroup indices (Ex. 10.11 & 10.15)
cards.body: In \(D_6\), \(\langle \rho^2 \rangle\) has order \(3\). In \(S_5\), \(\sigma = (1,2,5,4)(2,3) = (1,2,3,5,4)\) is a \(5\)-cycle of order \(5\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is every group \(G\) of prime order \(p\) cyclic (Corollary 10.8)?
options: Any \(a \neq e\) generates \(\langle a \rangle\) of order \(m \ge 2\) dividing \(p\), so \(m = p\) and \(\langle a \rangle = G\)
Every finite group has an element of order equal to \(|G|\)
cards.why: Since \(p\) is prime and \(|\langle a \rangle| \ge 2\) divides \(p\) by Lagrange's Theorem, \(|\langle a \rangle| = p\), so \(\langle a \rangle = G\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Let \(G\) be a group of order \(pq\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are prime numbers (Exercise 10.36). What must be true of every proper subgroup \(H < G\)?
options: \(H\) is cyclic because its order must be \(1\), \(p\), or \(q\)
cards.why: By Lagrange's Theorem, a proper subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) has order \(1\), \(p\), or \(q\). The trivial group and groups of prime order are all cyclic.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Definition 10.10, the number of left cosets of a subgroup \(H\) in a group \(G\) is called the ______ of \(H\) in \(G\), denoted \((G : H)\).
cards.why: Definition 10.10 defines the index \((G : H)\) as the number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Let \(\mu = (1, 2, 4, 5)(3, 6)\) in \(S_6\) (Exercise 10.16). Find the index \((S_6 : \langle \mu \rangle)\).
cards.why: The disjoint cycles have lengths \(4\) and \(2\), so \(|\langle \mu \rangle| = \operatorname{lcm}(4, 2) = 4\). Thus \((S_6 : \langle \mu \rangle) = 6! / 4 = 720 / 4 = 180\).
